messages.subject: Re: correlates of detectability
parts:
Alex-

I'm replying to the list as well as these are the types of questions
that others may have as well, so it is good to post these. Also, if you
post to the list then others may be able to respond if I don't.

My advice is simple. If you are able to construct good regression
models using body size and call frequency with ESW=p*W, then you should
incorporate those covariates into your MCDS model and use them along
with distance to predict p for all of your species including those with
few detections. That will be a much more direct way to solve the problem.

--jeff

On 3/16/2010 6:28 PM, Alex Anderson wrote:
> > Hi Jeff,
> > Thanks to your earlier help, I am making some progress with
> > understanding detection function variations in my data using MCDS.
> > While I think I am getting on top of that issue following your
> > advice, I am also tackling another question which would like your
> > opinion on if you have time. In my distance sampling data set for
> > forest birds, some species are inevitably too infrequently encountered
> > to generate meaningful estimates of density from my distance data.
> > Thus I have some good distance-based empirical density estimates for
> > some species, while the rest remain as only indices of relative
> > abundance. I am wondering however if there might be a way to arrive at
> > some compromise estimates? The approach I am taking at present is to
> > look at the relationship between effective strip width (ESW) or
> > detection probability (P) and species characteristics such as body
> > mass and the dominant frequency of their call or song. I have so far
> > been able to build some decent multiple regresion models in this way.
> > My plan is to use that to predict the ESW for species for which my
> > data are insufficient for direct estimation. the process i have been
> > using is basically: estimate ESw for as many species as possible,
> > generate the multiple regression model, predict ESW for the remaining
> > species, and then multiply their truncated raw count data by twice
> > the predicted effective strip width times my transect length.
> > Provided the raw count data are A) truncated at the same distance as
> > the data used to generate the predictive model, and B) the species
> > lies within the range of values of physical parameters used to
> > generate the model (ie, interpolation not extrapolation), My
> > question is whether effective strip width and their raw count data can
> > be used in this way to generate density estimates? should I be using
> > detection probability instead? any thoughts would be much appreciated.
> > regards
